title: Pediatric Dehydration Assessment & Oral Rehydration Therapy
keywords: clinical assessment beats any specific lab value for grading dehydration severity in a child, general appearance, capillary refill, skin turgor, and mucous membranes together outperform a single sign alone

purpose: Clinical dehydration severity assessment and the oral-rehydration-first approach (including ondansetron-facilitated ORT) for the far-more-common-than-DKA pediatric gastroenteritis/dehydration presentation.
ageRange: Infants through school-age children; ORT principles apply broadly but younger infants carry less physiologic reserve and warrant closer monitoring.

body.text: Clinical assessment — no single sign, no lab value beats the combination

Dehydration severity in a child is graded clinically — general appearance/alertness, capillary refill time, skin turgor, and mucous membrane moisture together, not any single sign or a specific lab value in isolation. Clinical assessment using this combination of signs has been shown to outperform isolated measures (including a single lab value) for estimating actual fluid deficit.

rows: Alert, normal vital signs, moist mucous membranes, normal capillary refill
No specific rehydration needed beyond continued normal intake
Slightly decreased activity, dry mucous membranes, normal-to-mildly-delayed capillary refill, normal-to-mildly-decreased urine output
ORAL REHYDRATION THERAPY is FIRST-LINE — not a fallback after IV access fails
Lethargy/altered mental status, delayed capillary refill, decreased skin turgor, minimal urine output, possible hemodynamic compromise
IV fluids first — ORT is not the initial approach for a severely dehydrated child

body.text: Oral rehydration therapy — first-line for mild-moderate, not a fallback

ORT is FIRST-LINE therapy for mild-to-moderate dehydration — it is not something to try only after IV access has failed or as a lesser alternative. Going straight to IV fluids in a child who could tolerate oral rehydration skips a genuinely effective, evidence-supported, and less invasive first step.

items: Use a proper oral rehydration solution (ORS) — the WHO formulation is roughly 75 mEq/L sodium and 75 mmol/L glucose, a specific balanced electrolyte/glucose composition. Sports drinks, juice, and soda are NOT adequate substitutes in a meaningfully dehydrated child — they carry too much sugar relative to electrolytes and can worsen osmotic diarrhea.
Give small, frequent volumes rather than large volumes at once, especially in a child who has been vomiting — this improves tolerance.
Reassess response over the ED visit — improving alertness, tolerance of oral intake, and urine output are the practical markers of successful rehydration.

body.text: Ondansetron-facilitated ORT — give it before writing off oral rehydration as failed

A single oral dose of ondansetron, given to a child with gastroenteritis-associated vomiting who is failing to tolerate oral rehydration, meaningfully reduces the need for IV rehydration and reduces continued vomiting — this is a well-studied, practice-changing intervention (used by the large majority of pediatric ED physicians for this indication).

The practical implication: before concluding that a child has 'failed' oral rehydration and needs IV fluids, give a dose of ondansetron and reattempt ORT — many children who would otherwise 'fail' oral intake succeed once vomiting is controlled.
When IV fluids are the right call

items: Severe dehydration (see table above) gets IV fluids as the initial approach, not a trial of ORT first.

A child who genuinely fails an adequate trial of ORT (including with ondansetron facilitation) — persistent vomiting, worsening clinical status, or inability to keep up with ongoing losses — needs IV rehydration.
Significant electrolyte derangement, altered mental status, or hemodynamic compromise are all reasons to move directly to IV fluids rather than attempting oral rehydration first.

Nasogastric rehydration is a reasonable intermediate option in some settings/patients who can't tolerate oral intake by mouth but don't yet need IV access — worth knowing as an option between ORT and IV fluids, per local practice.
